reasons_add: Ibn ʿĀshūr says the oath and emphatic particle strengthen the warning that loss envelops most people.

Ibn ʿĀshūr applies the comprehensive generic to people living when Islam appeared, especially those its call reached worldwide; the believer exception leaves the judgment true of others. Qurtubi calls the generic reading sound on account of the exception.
Ibn ʿĀshūr calls those in great loss polytheists.
Rāzī reports the Abu Jahl identification as attributed to the Prophet without stating a grading.
Qurtubi reports al-Dahhak's group as including al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and al-As ibn Wa'il.

question: 103:2/q02
position: A previously known individual, left unidentified in this grammatical alternative.
reasons: Razi says the definite article may point to a previously known individual, as an alternative to denoting the human class.

reasons_add: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the generic definite customarily comprehensive, qualified by the believer exception.
Qurtubi explicitly prefers the community's codices and says wording opposed to the Uthmanic codex is not Qur'an for recitation.
Qurtubi explains the damma as vowel-following.

Ibn Atiyya also reports Ali's shorter opening variant, 'By the vicissitudes of time, mankind is in loss.' Durr relates Ibn Masud's time's-end wording through Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim, and Abd Allah ibn Utba; Abd Allah ibn Utba affirms it against Bishr ibn Marwan's accusation of disbelief.
Razi adds that the emphatic lam works with inna; Ibn ʿĀshūr says figurative containment is stronger than simply calling someone a loser.
Ibn ʿĀshūr relates magnification to the threatening context of the oath.
Alusi calls it a kind of loss unfamiliar to people; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows multiple kinds and comprehensiveness.
Ibn ʿĀshūr treats loss as the opposite of trading profit and compares an unprofitable trade in 2:16. Ibn Atiyya includes a bad condition among its senses.
Qurtubi says loss, destruction, punishment, evil and deficiency are close in meaning.
Ibn Atiyya adds that believers' age and worldly hardship are forgiven beside everlasting afterlife profit.
Ibn Atiyya says this is clearest in a disbeliever and calls it manifest loss.

question: 103:2/q07
position: An adverse afterlife outcome rather than a verdict on worldly fortune.
reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr says trade loss metaphorically names the bad end awaiting one who expects bliss; the warning concerns the future, especially the eternal afterlife, not worldly turns of fortune (3:196–197).

reasons_add: Baydawi and Alusi say people spend life in pursuits that yield no afterlife benefit; Alusi adds possible harm at resurrection. Biqai stresses attachment to the passing present.
Biqai describes loss as driven by whims, personal aims and delusion about what passes away; Ibn al-Zubayr connects innate injustice and ignorance in 33:72.
Kashshaf describes the righteous as buying the afterlife with this world and gaining happiness; Abu Hayyan says the reverse transaction is the greatest loss.
Ibn Atiyya says believers' temporary hardship is forgiven beside lasting success; Ibrāhīm says their youthful deeds continue to be credited in decline.

Alusi says one outside the exception need not face eternal Fire: an unpardoned sinner may enter Fire, while a pardoned one may lose higher ranks. He calls other, unspecified replies offered by al-Maturidi strained.

Baydawi says the oath indirectly denies that time causes loss; Alusi places responsibility on people amid time's blessings and opposites, while calling an identification of ʿasr with dahr unclear. Biqai associates ʿasr with time's essence and the extraction of essences.
Tabari and Mawardi report Ali's reading of the oath as time's vicissitudes.
Ibn al-Zubayr also connects the exception to those whose trade does not distract them in 24:37.
Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the unprofitable trade of 2:16 and cites 3:196–197 against judging by worldly fortune.
Biqai calls humanity the noblest species because it was made in the best form, and relates the root of ʿasr to extracting an essence.
Durr attributes the Companion practice to Abu Mulayka al-Darimi.
Qurtubi also reports Ibn Abbas preaching the assignments as a Companion report.
Ibn Kathir places the exchange after Muhammad's mission and before Amr ibn al-As converted; Amr called Musaylima a liar.
Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes people living when Islam appeared, especially those reached by its call worldwide.

question: Why does the warning of human loss imply a need for messengers?

positions.position: Messengers explain the beliefs, worship and customs God approves so people can persist in faith and Islam.
positions.reasons: Biqai draws this need from humanity's loss and its susceptibility to error.
